title: What Pete Buttigieg’s Bet in the 2026 Midterms Could Mean for 2028
summary: No longer a fresh face, he is arguing that his party needs moderate red-state whisperers.

Not long after **Jamie Ager** , a farmer in Western North Carolina and a Democrat, announced a long-shot run for Congress, his phone rang. **Pete Buttigieg** was on the line, offering to help.


It was the summer of 2025, long before national Democrats realized they had a shot at winning districts like Ager’s, which President Trump carried by nearly 10 percentage points in 2024. But it was exactly the kind of place Buttigieg wanted to plant a flag — and Ager’s campaign was happy to have him, even as it kept its distance from most national Democrats.


“People don’t hate him,” **Grayson Barnette** , Ager’s campaign manager, said. “Right?”


The 2026 midterms were not exactly primed to be the Year of Pete. He passed on running for Senate in Michigan. His association with the Biden administration, in which he served for four years as transportation secretary, was hardly a boon in a party desperate to move on. He was neither a governor nor a member of Congress with a built-in platform.


But seven years after Buttigieg, then the mayor of South Bend, Ind., made himself an unavoidable fixture of Democratic politics by running in the 2020 presidential election, he made himself an unavoidable fixture of the midterm campaign trail. He campaigned for more than 100 candidates in person, often in traditionally conservative states like Oklahoma, Kansas, Texas and Mississippi. He felt his party was too quick to pass over such places — and believed Trump’s unpopularity had handed Democrats an unusual opportunity in them.


Those ventures could give Buttigieg new allies as he considers a second presidential run, a decision he will make early next year, according to a person familiar with his thinking. And the results, which included a victory for Ager, have set him up to argue that what a party dazzled by progressives and fresher faces really needs is a moderate red-state whisperer like himself.


“The broader mistake I was worried about the party making was not paying enough attention to these redder areas, which is why I made a point of paying a lot of attention to them,” Buttigieg said in an interview.
